extraction_notes.note: Tagged optimization formulations ((P), (G), (G'), (DG'), (Q), ...) are equation facts retyped as problem by content; the ones inside proofs ((G''), (DG'')) were kept as equation.
Numbered equations (2.x/4.x) stating the cited GM and FGM convergence rates were retyped as external theorems since the text presents them as proved results of others.

The text says the feasibility of (BIL) follows from the proof of Theorem \ref{T:gradLowBound} (3.2), but the explicit dual feasible point is in the proof of Theorem 3.1; an inferred edge from PP3 was added besides the ref edge.

Algorithms are written as enumerated lists inside \fbox, not algorithm environments; steps were segmented by hand. Algorithm FGM' (AP5) was given no steps because its lines nest inside an itemize whose spans overlap the surrounding sentence.
Numerical tables of bounds (Figures 2, 3) and the N=5 optimal-step algorithm (Figure 4) are figure content and were not extracted as nodes; their summaries are numerical claims ClP4, ClP5, ClP7.
The PEP (P) is displayed twice (introduction with $f\in\mathcal{F}$, Section 2.2 with $f$ convex $C^{1,1}_L$); treated as one problem with the introduction copy in also_stated_at.

nodes.name: First-order black-box optimization method
nodes.statement:
According to this model, a \emph{first-order black-box} optimization
method is an algorithm which has knowledge of the underlying space $\mathbb{R}^d$ and the family
$\mathcal{F}$, the function itself is not known.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia:
has knowledge of the underlying space $\mathbb{R}^d$ and the family
$\mathcal{F}$

nodes.name: First-order oracle
nodes.statement:
To gain information on the function to be
minimized, the algorithm  queries a first order oracle, that is, a subroutine which given as
input a point in $\mathbb{R}^d$, returns the value of the objective function and its gradient at
that point.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia:
given as
input a point in $\mathbb{R}^d$, returns the value of the objective function and its gradient at
that point

nodes.name: Iteration rule of a first-order algorithm
nodes.statement:
The algorithm thus generates a finite sequence of points $\{x_i\in \mathbb{R}^d :
i=0,\dots,N\}$, where at each step the algorithm can depend only on the previous steps, their
function values and gradients via some rule
$$
 
 x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d,\; x_{i+1}={\cal A}(x_0,\dots,x_i; f(x_0),\dots,f(x_i); f'(x_0),\dots, f'(x_i)), \; i=0, \ldots, N-1,
$$
where $f'(\cdot)$ stands for the gradient of $f(\cdot)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: A first-order method generates $x_0,\dots,x_N$ where each $x_{i+1}$ depends only on previous points, function values and gradients.

nodes.name: epsilon-optimal solution
nodes.statement:
Given a desired accuracy $\varepsilon >0$, applying the given algorithm on the function $f$ in
the class $\mathcal{F}$, the algorithm stops when it produces an approximate solution
$x_\varepsilon$ which is $\varepsilon$-optimal, that is such that $$f(x_\epsilon) - f(x_\ast)
\leq \epsilon.$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Absolute inaccuracy
nodes.statement:
Equivalently, we can measure the performance of an algorithm by looking
at the absolute inaccuracy $$ \delta(f,x_N) = f(x_N) - f(x_\ast),$$ where $x_N$ is the result
of the algorithm after making $N$ calls to the oracle.

nodes.name: Smooth unconstrained convex minimization (M)
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $f$ over $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a first-order algorithm $\mathcal{A}$.

nodes.name: Convex function with L-Lipschitz gradient
nodes.statement:
$f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$  is a convex function of the type $C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$, i.e.,
continuously differentiable with Lipschitz continuous gradient:
\[
    \|f'(x)-f'(y)\|\leq L \|x-y\|,\,\,\forall x,y\in \mathbb{R}^d,
\]
where $L>0$ is the Lipschitz constant.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is convex and in $C^{1,1}_L$: continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient.

nodes.name: Solvability of (M)
nodes.statement:
We assume that (M) is solvable, i.e., the optimal set $X_*(f):=arg\,min f$ is nonempty, and for
$x_*\in X_*(f)$ we set $f^*:=f(x_*).$
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Bounded distance to an optimal solution
nodes.statement:
There exists $R>0$, such that

the distance from $x_0$ to an optimal solution $x_\ast\in X_*(f)$ is bounded by
$R$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Performance Estimation Problem (PEP)
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Idea and Main Approach
nodes.statement_short: Worst-case absolute inaccuracy $f(x_N)-f(x_*)$ of algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ over all convex $C^{1,1}_L$ functions and starting points within distance $R$.
nodes.label: P:baseproblem

nodes.name: Relaxation idea for the PEP
nodes.statement:
An un-formal description of the underlying idea consists of two main steps as follows:

\begin{itemize}
\item Given an algorithm ${\cal A}$ that generates a finite sequence of points,

to build a problem in finite dimension we
replace the functional constraint $f\in C^{1,1}_L$ in \eqref{P:baseproblem} by new variables in $\mathbb{R}^d$. These
variables, are the points $\{x_0, x_1, \ldots x_N, x_\ast \}$ themselves, the function values
and their gradients at these points. Roughly speaking, this can be seen as a sort of
discretization of $f$ at a selected set of points.
\item To define constraints that relate the new variables, we use relevant/useful
properties characterizing the family of convex functions in $C^{1,1}_L$, as well as the
rule(s) describing the given algorithm ${\cal A}$.
\end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Idea and Main Approach
nodes.statement_short: Replace the functional constraint by finitely many variables (points, values, gradients) linked by $C^{1,1}_L$ convexity inequalities and the algorithm's rule.

nodes.name: Relaxations of the PEP give valid upper bounds
nodes.statement:
Note that any
relaxation performed on the maximization problem \eqref{P:baseproblem} may increase its
optimal value, however, the optimal value of the relaxed problem still remains a valid upper
bound on $f(x_N)-f^\ast$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Idea and Main Approach
assumptions:
any
relaxation performed on the maximization problem \eqref{P:baseproblem}
conclusions:
the optimal value of the relaxed problem still remains a valid upper
bound on $f(x_N)-f^\ast$

nodes.name: Relaxed PEP for the gradient method
nodes.statement:
Problem \eqref{P:baseproblem} can now be
relaxed by \emph{discarding} the underlying function $f \in C^{1,1}_L$ in
\eqref{P:baseproblem}. That is, the constraint in the function space $f\in C^{1,1}_L$ with $f$
convex, is replaced by the inequalities (\ref{carf}) characterizing this family of functions
and expressed in terms of the variables $x_0,\dots,x_N,x_\ast\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
$g_0,\dots,g_N\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\delta_0,\dots,\delta_N\in\mathbb{R}$ generated by (GM).
Thus, an upper bound on the worst case behavior of $f(x_N)-f(x_\ast)= L \|x_\ast -x_0\|^2
\delta_N$
 can be obtained by solving the following relaxed PEP:
\begin{align*}
    
    \max_{\substack{x_0,\dots,x_N,x_\ast\in\mathbb{R}^d,\\g_0,\dots,g_N\in\mathbb{R}^d,\\\delta_0,\dots,\delta_N \in\mathbb{R}}}\ & L\|x_\ast-x_0\|^2 \delta_N \\
    \text{s.t. }\quad
                        & x_{i+1} = x_i - h \|x_\ast-x_0\| g_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N-1,\\
                        & \frac{1}{2}\| g_i - g_j \| ^2 \leq \delta_i - \delta_j - \frac{ \langle g_j, x_i-x_j \rangle}{\|x_\ast-x_0\|},\quad  i,j=0,\dots,N,\ast, \\
                        &\|x_\ast-x_0\|\leq R.
\end{align*}

nodes.name: Dimension reduction for quadratic matrix functions
nodes.statement:
Let $f(X)=\mathrm{tr} (X^T Q X + 2 ba^T X)$ be a quadratic function, where $X\in
\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, $Q\in \mathbb{S}^n$, $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0\neq b\in
\mathbb{R}^m$. Then
\[
    \inf_{X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}} f(X) = \inf_{\xi\in \mathbb{R}^n} f(\xi b^T).
\]
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
assumptions:
$f(X)=\mathrm{tr} (X^T Q X + 2 ba^T X)$ be a quadratic function, where $X\in
\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, $Q\in \mathbb{S}^n$, $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0\neq b\in
\mathbb{R}^m$
conclusions: \inf_{X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}} f(X) = \inf_{\xi\in \mathbb{R}^n} f(\xi b^T).
nodes.statement_short: The infimum of $\mathrm{tr}(X^TQX+2ba^TX)$ over matrices equals that over rank-one $X=\xi b^T$.
nodes.label: L:quadlemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement:
First, we recall (this can be easily verified) that $\inf \{f(X): X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\}
>-\infty$ if and only if $Q \succeq 0$, and there exists at least one solution ${\bar X}$ such
that
\begin{equation} Q{\bar X}+ ab^T=0 \;
\Leftrightarrow\; {\bar X}^TQ +ba^T=0,
\end{equation}
i.e., the above is just $\nabla f (X)= 0$ and characterizes the minimizers of the convex
function $f(X)$. Using (\ref{s1}) it follows that $\inf_X f(X)=f({\bar X})=\mathrm{tr} (ba^T{\bar
X})$.
 Now, for any $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we have $f(\xi b^T)=\|b\|^2(\xi^TQ\xi + 2a^T\xi)$. Thus, likewise,
 $\inf\{f(\xi b^T): \xi \in \mathbb{R}^n\} >-\infty$ if and only if $Q \succeq 0$ and there exists ${\bar \xi}\in \mathbb{R}^n$ such
that \begin{equation} Q{\bar \xi} + a=0,\end{equation} and using (\ref{s2}) it
follows $\inf_\xi f(\xi b^T)=f({\bar \xi}b^T)=\|b\|^2a^T{\bar \xi}=\mathrm{tr} (ba^T{\bar
\xi}b^T)$. Now, using (\ref{s1})-(\ref{s2}), one obtains ${\bar X}^TQ=-ba^T$ and $Q({\bar X}-
{\bar \xi}b^T)=0$, and hence it follows that
\begin{eqnarray*}
f({\bar X})-f({\bar \xi})&=&\mathrm{tr} (ba^T({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T))\\
                        &=&\mathrm{tr} (-{\bar X}^TQ({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T)=0.
                        \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.statement:
For convenience,  we recast \eqref{P:gpr} as a minimization problem, and we also omit the
fixed term $LR^2$ from the objective. That is, we consider the equivalent problem \eqref{P:agpr}
defined by
\begin{align*}
    \begin{aligned}
    \min_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta \in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\ &  -\delta_N \\
    \text{s.t. }
                        & \mathrm{tr} (G^T A_{i-1,i} G) \leq \delta_{i-1} - \delta_i,\quad    i=1,\dots,N, \\
                        & \mathrm{tr}(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad     i=0,\dots,N.
    \end{aligned}
    \tag{G$^{\prime\prime}$} \end{align*}

Attaching the dual multipliers $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N) \in \mathbb{R}^N_{+}$ and
$\tau:=(\tau_0, \ldots ,\tau_N)^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}_{+}$ to the first and second set of
inequalities respectively, and using the notation $\delta=(\delta_0, \ldots ,\delta_N)$, we
get that the Lagrangian of this problem is given as a sum of two separable functions in the
variables $(\delta, G)$:
\begin{eqnarray*}
    L(G,\delta, \lambda, \tau)&=&
        
        
         -\delta_N+\sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i(\delta_i - \delta_{i-1}) + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i \delta_i \\
         & &+ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i \mathrm{tr}(G^T A_{i-1,i} G)+ \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i
        \left( \mathrm{tr}(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G) \right)\\
        & \equiv & L_1(\delta, \lambda, \tau)+ L_2(G,\lambda, \tau).
\end{eqnarray*}
The dual objective function is then defined by $$H(\lambda, \tau)=\min_{G, \delta} L(G,\delta,
\lambda\, \tau)=\min_\delta L_1(\delta, \lambda, \tau)+ \min_{G} L_2(G, \lambda, \tau),$$ and
the dual problem of \eqref{P:agpr} is then given by
\begin{align*}
    \begin{aligned}
        \max \{ H(\lambda, \tau):\; \lambda \in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{+}, \tau \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}_{+}\}.
    \end{aligned}
    \tag{DG$^{\prime\prime}$} \end{align*}
Since $L_1(\cdot,\lambda, \tau)$ is linear in $\delta$, we have $\min_\delta
L_1(\delta,\lambda, \tau) =0$ whenever
\begin{eqnarray}
            -\lambda_1 +\tau_0 &= & 0, \nonumber\\
            \lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}+\tau_i &=& 0\quad (i=1,\dots,N-1), \\
             -1+\lambda_N+\tau_N &=& 0, \nonumber
            \end{eqnarray}
            and $-\infty$ otherwise. Invoking Lemma~\ref{L:quadlemma}, we get
\begin{align*}
     \min_{G\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d}} L_2(G,\lambda, \tau) =
     \min_{w\in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}} L_2(w \nu^T,\lambda, \tau).
\end{align*}
Therefore for any $(\lambda,\tau)$ satisfying (\ref{eqtau}), we have obtained that the dual
objective reduces to
\begin{eqnarray*}
 H(\lambda, \tau) &=& \min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\{w^T \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i  A_{i-1,i}  +
        \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i  D_i \right) w + \tau^T w \}\\
        &=&  \max_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \{-\frac{1}{2}t :
        w^T \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i  A_{i-1,i}  +
        \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i  D_i \right) w + \tau^T w \leq -\frac{1}{2}t,\ \forall w\in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}
        \}\\
 &=& \max_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \left\{
            -\frac{1}{2}t:
            \begin{pmatrix}
                \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i  A_{i-1,i}  + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i  D_i  & \frac{1}{2} \tau \\
                \frac{1}{2}\tau^T       & \frac{1}{2}t
        \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0
        \right\}.
\end{eqnarray*}
where the last equality follows from  the well known lemma
\cite[Page~163]{ben2001lectures}\footnote{Let $M$ be a symmetric matrix. Then, $x^TMx + 2 b^Tx+ c \geq 0, \forall x \in
\mathbb{R}^d$ if and only if the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} M & b\\ b^T & c \end{pmatrix}$ is positive
semidefinite.}.

Now, recalling the definition of the matrices $A_{i-1,i}, D_i$ (see
(\ref{E:gradientmatrices})), we obtain {\small
\[
    \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i  A_{i-1,i}  =
    \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
        \lambda_1       & (h-1)\lambda_1            \\
        (h-1)\lambda_1          & \lambda_1+\lambda_2   & (h-1)\lambda_2                \\
            &       (h-1)\lambda_2          & \lambda_2 +\lambda_3  & (h-1)\lambda_3                \\
                                    &        & \ddots        &\ddots &   \ddots\\
                                            & &                 &       (h-1)\lambda_{N-1}  & \lambda_{N-1}+ \lambda_N & (h-1)\lambda_N \\
                                            & &                 &        &  (h-1)\lambda_N  & \lambda_N\\
    \end{pmatrix}
    \]
    }
and {\small
\[
    \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i  D_i =
    \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix}
        \tau_0          & h\tau_1           & \dots     &h\tau_{N-1}    &h\tau_N  \\
        h\tau_1             & \tau_1        &               &h\tau_{N-1}    &h\tau_N \\

        \vdots  & & \ddots &     &\vdots \\
        h\tau_{N-1}     & h\tau_{N-1}   &           & \tau_{N-1}        & h\tau_N \\
        h\tau_N         & h\tau_N & \dots       & h\tau_N   & \tau_N \\
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]
}
Finally,  using the relations (\ref{eqtau}) to eliminate $\tau_i$, and recalling that
$\mathrm{val}\!\eqref{P:agpr}$ was defined as $-LR^2 \mathrm{val}\!\eqref{P:gpr}$, the desired form of the stated dual problem
follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
First note that both (G) and \eqref{P:gpr} are clearly feasible 
and $\mathrm{val} (G) \leq\mathrm{val}\eqref{P:gpr}$.
Invoking Lemma \ref{lem:dual}, by weak duality for the pair of primal-dual problems
\eqref{P:gpr} and \eqref{P:dualgpr}, we thus obtain that $\mathrm{val}\eqref{P:gpr}\leq \mathrm{val}\eqref{P:dualgpr}$

and hence:
\begin{equation} f(x_N)-f^* \leq \mathrm{val} (G) \leq \mathrm{val} \eqref{P:gpr} \leq \mathrm{val} \eqref{P:dualgpr}.
\end{equation}

Now consider the following point $(\lambda,t)$ for the dual problem \eqref{P:dualgpr}:
\begin{align*}
    \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N,  \\
    t   &= \frac{1}{2Nh+1}.
\end{align*}
Assuming that this point is \eqref{P:dualgpr}-feasible, it follows from (\ref{weak}) that
$$
f(x_N)-f^* \leq \mathrm{val}\eqref{P:dualgpr} \leq \frac{L R^2}{4 N h+2},
$$
which proves the desired result. Thus, it remains to show that the above given choice
$(\lambda, t)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:dualgpr}. First, it is easy to see that all the linear constraints
of \eqref{P:dualgpr} on the variables $\lambda_i, i=1,\ldots ,N$ described through the set $\Lambda$
hold true. Now we prove that the matrix $S\equiv S(\lambda,t)$ is positive semidefinite. From
Lemma~\ref{L:positivedefinitea0a1}, with $h \in [0,1]$, we get that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1$ is
positive definite, as a convex combination of positive definite matrices. Next, we argue that
the determinant of $S$ is zero. Indeed, take $u:=(1,\dots,1,-(2Nh+1))^T$, then from the
definition of $S$ and the choice of $\lambda_i$ and $t$ it follows by elementary algebra that
$Su=0$. To complete the argument, we note that the determinant of $S$ can also be found via
the identity (see, e.g., \cite[Section~A.5.5]{boyd2004}):
\[
    \det(S) = (t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q) \det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1).
\]
Since we have just shown that  $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1 \succ 0$, then $\det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)>0$ and
we get from the above identity that the value of $t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q$, which is the
Schur complement of the matrix $S$, is equal to 0. By a well known lemma on the Schur
complement \cite[Lemma~4.2.1]{ben2001lectures}, we conclude that $S$ is positive semidefinite.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.2
nodes.statement:
We will describe two functions that attain the two parts of the $\max$ expression in the above
claimed statement. For the sake of simplicity we will

assume that 
$L=1$ and $R=\|x_\ast-x_0\|=1$.
Generalizing this proof to general values of $L$ and $R$
can be done by an appropriate scaling.

To show the first part of the $\max$ expression, consider the function

\[
    \varphi_1(x) =
    \begin{cases}
        \frac{1}{2Nh+1} \|x\| -\frac{1}{2(2Nh+1)^2}       &   \| x \| \geq \frac{1}{2Nh+1} \\
        \frac{1}{2} \|x\|^2         &   \| x\| < \frac{1}{2Nh+1}
    \end{cases}.
\]
Note that this function is nothing else but the Moreau proximal envelope of the function
$\frac{1}{2Nh+1}\|x\|$, \cite{M65}. It is well known that this function is convex, continuously
differentiable with Lipschitz constant $L=1$, and that its minimal value $\varphi(x_*)=0$, see
e.g., \cite{M65, rock-wets-book98}. Applying the gradient method on $\varphi_1(x)$ with
$x_0=\nu$ where, as before, $\nu$ is a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we obtain that for $i=0,\dots,N$:
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \varphi_1^\prime(x_i) &=& \frac{1}{2N h+1}\nu;\;  x_i = \left(1-\frac{i h}{2N h+1}\right)\nu,\\
 \mbox{and}\; \varphi_1(x_i) &=&  \frac{1}{2N h+1}\left(1-\frac{h i}{2N h+1} \right)-\frac{1}{2(2N h+1)^2}\\
 &=& \frac{1}{4Nh+2} \left(\frac{4Nh+1-2hi}{2Nh+1}\right).
 \end{eqnarray*}
Therefore,
\[
    \varphi_1(x_N)-\varphi_1(x_\ast)  = \varphi_1(x_N) = \frac{1}{4 N h+2}.
\]
To show the second part of the $\max$ expression, we apply the gradient method on
\[
    \varphi_2(x) = \frac{1}{2} \|x\|^2
\]
with $x_0=\nu$. We then get that for $i=0,\dots,N$:
$$
    \varphi_2^\prime(x_i)= x_i;\;  x_i =(1-h)^i \nu;\; \varphi_2(x_i) = \frac{1}{2}(1-h)^{2i},
$$
and hence
\[
    \varphi_2(x_N)-\varphi_2(x_\ast) = \varphi_2(x_N) = \frac{1}{2} (1-h)^{2N}
\]
and the desired claim is proven.

nodes.name: Optimal constant step size under Conjecture 3.1
nodes.statement:
Assuming the above conjecture holds true,
the optimal step size (i.e., the step size that produces the best complexity bound)
for the gradient method with constant step size
is given by the unique positive solution to the equation $$\frac{1}{2 N
h+1}=(1-h)^{2N}.$$

The solution of this equation approaches $2$ as $N$ grows. Therefore, assuming the conjecture
holds true and $N$ is large enough, the complexity of the gradient method with the optimal
step size approaches~$\frac{LR^2}{8 N+2}$.

nodes.statement_short: If the conjecture holds, the best constant step solves $1/(2Nh+1)=(1-h)^{2N}$, tends to 2, giving bound about $LR^2/(8N+2)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement:
We will show by induction that the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace is
identical to the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM}\xspace, and that the value of
$x_N$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace is equal to the value of $x_N$ generated by
Algorithm~\text{FGM}\xspace.

First note that the sequence $t_i$ is defined by the two algorithms in the same way. Now let
$\{x_i$, $y_i\}$ be the sequences generated by \text{FGM}\xspace and denote by $\{y_i^\prime\}$,
$x_N^\prime$ the sequence generated by \text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace. Obviously, $y^\prime_1 = y_1$ and since
$t_1=1$ we get using the relations \ref{E:nesterovsteps}:
\begin{align*}
    y_2^\prime &= y_1^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(2)}_1 f^\prime(y_1^\prime) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} \left(1+\frac{t_{1}-1}{t_2} \right) f^\prime(y_1) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_1)= x_1 = y_2.
\end{align*}
Assuming $y_i^\prime = y_i$ for $i = 1,\dots,n$, we then have
\begin{align*}
    y_{n+1}^\prime &= y_n^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_n f^\prime(y_n^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_{n-1} f^\prime(y_{n-1}^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} h^{(n+1)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\
        &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} (1+\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}) f^\prime(y_n) - \frac{1}{L} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}(h^{(n)}_{n-1}-1) f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\
        &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L}  f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime)\right) \\
        &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L}  f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) +y_n^\prime-y_{n-1}^\prime\right) \\
        &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} (x_n-x_{n-1}) \\
        &= y_{n+1}.
\end{align*}
Finally,
\[
    x_N^\prime = y_N^\prime -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N^\prime) = y_N -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N) = x_N.
\]

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.1
nodes.statement:
As (LIN) is a relaxation of \eqref{P:pblin}, it is enough to show that \eqref{P:pblin} can achieve the same
objective value. Let $(r^\ast,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ be an optimal solution
for (LIN). If $\lambda_i^\ast \neq 0$ for all $1\leq i \leq N$, then~\eqref{E:solvebil}
satisfies all the equations in \eqref{E:definex} and therefore
$(h,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:pblin}.

Suppose $\lambda^\ast_m=0$ for some $1\leq m \leq N$ and that $m$ is the maximal index with
this property. Then by the equality and non-negativity constraints in (LIN), we get that
$\lambda^\ast_1=\lambda^\ast_2=\dots=\lambda^\ast_m=0$ and
$\tau^\ast_0=\tau^\ast_1=\dots=\tau^\ast_{m-1}=0$.
Let $S:=S(r,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast)$, then by the positive semidefinite constraint in (LIN), we have $S \succeq 0$.
From the linear equalities connecting $\lambda$ and $\tau$ it follows that
\[
    S_{i,i}=\begin{cases}
            \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_1^\ast+\tau_0^\ast) = \lambda_1^\ast, &\quad i=1 \\
            \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_i^\ast+\lambda_{i-1}^\ast+\tau_{i-1}^\ast) = \lambda_i^\ast, &\quad i=2,\dots,N
        \end{cases},
\]
and we get that $S_{1,1}=\dots=S_{m,m}=0$. By the properties of positive semidefinite matrices we now get that $r_{i,k}^\ast=0$ for $i=1,\dots,m$ and $k=0,\dots,i-1$,
hence the set of equations \eqref{E:definex} with the chosen values of $h_k^{(i)}$ is consistent.

nodes.name: Lagrangian
nodes.statement:
Attaching the dual multipliers $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N) \in \mathbb{R}^N_{+}$ and
$\tau:=(\tau_0, \ldots ,\tau_N)^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}_{+}$ to the first and second set of
inequalities respectively, and using the notation $\delta=(\delta_0, \ldots ,\delta_N)$, we
get that the Lagrangian of this problem is given as a sum of two separable functions in the
variables $(\delta, G)$:
\begin{eqnarray*}
    L(G,\delta, \lambda, \tau)&=&
        
        
         -\delta_N+\sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i(\delta_i - \delta_{i-1}) + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i \delta_i \\
         & &+ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i \mathrm{tr}(G^T A_{i-1,i} G)+ \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i
        \left( \mathrm{tr}(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G) \right)\\
        & \equiv & L_1(\delta, \lambda, \tau)+ L_2(G,\lambda, \tau).
\end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Minimize linear part
nodes.statement:
Since $L_1(\cdot,\lambda, \tau)$ is linear in $\delta$, we have $\min_\delta
L_1(\delta,\lambda, \tau) =0$ whenever
\begin{eqnarray}
            -\lambda_1 +\tau_0 &= & 0, \nonumber\\
            \lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}+\tau_i &=& 0\quad (i=1,\dots,N-1), \\
             -1+\lambda_N+\tau_N &=& 0, \nonumber
            \end{eqnarray}
            and $-\infty$ otherwise.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: The $\delta$-part is finite only under linear relations (eqtau).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.1
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Reduce minimization over $G$ to rank-one $w\nu^T$.

nodes.name: LMI form of the dual objective
nodes.statement:
Therefore for any $(\lambda,\tau)$ satisfying (\ref{eqtau}), we have obtained that the dual
objective reduces to
\begin{eqnarray*}
 H(\lambda, \tau) &=& \min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\{w^T \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i  A_{i-1,i}  +
        \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i  D_i \right) w + \tau^T w \}\\
        &=&  \max_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \{-\frac{1}{2}t :
        w^T \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i  A_{i-1,i}  +
        \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i  D_i \right) w + \tau^T w \leq -\frac{1}{2}t,\ \forall w\in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}
        \}\\
 &=& \max_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \left\{
            -\frac{1}{2}t:
            \begin{pmatrix}
                \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i  A_{i-1,i}  + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i  D_i  & \frac{1}{2} \tau \\
                \frac{1}{2}\tau^T       & \frac{1}{2}t
        \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0
        \right\}.
\end{eqnarray*}
where the last equality follows from  the well known lemma
\cite[Page~163]{ben2001lectures}\footnote{Let $M$ be a symmetric matrix. Then, $x^TMx + 2 b^Tx+ c \geq 0, \forall x \in
\mathbb{R}^d$ if and only if the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} M & b\\ b^T & c \end{pmatrix}$ is positive
semidefinite.}.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Express $H$ as a max over $t$ subject to an LMI via the PSD characterization of nonnegative quadratics.

nodes.name: Compute the matrices
nodes.statement:
Now, recalling the definition of the matrices $A_{i-1,i}, D_i$ (see
(\ref{E:gradientmatrices})), we obtain {\small
\[
    \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i  A_{i-1,i}  =
    \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
        \lambda_1       & (h-1)\lambda_1            \\
        (h-1)\lambda_1          & \lambda_1+\lambda_2   & (h-1)\lambda_2                \\
            &       (h-1)\lambda_2          & \lambda_2 +\lambda_3  & (h-1)\lambda_3                \\
                                    &        & \ddots        &\ddots &   \ddots\\
                                            & &                 &       (h-1)\lambda_{N-1}  & \lambda_{N-1}+ \lambda_N & (h-1)\lambda_N \\
                                            & &                 &        &  (h-1)\lambda_N  & \lambda_N\\
    \end{pmatrix}
    \]
    }
and {\small
\[
    \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i  D_i =
    \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix}
        \tau_0          & h\tau_1           & \dots     &h\tau_{N-1}    &h\tau_N  \\
        h\tau_1             & \tau_1        &               &h\tau_{N-1}    &h\tau_N \\

        \vdots  & & \ddots &     &\vdots \\
        h\tau_{N-1}     & h\tau_{N-1}   &           & \tau_{N-1}        & h\tau_N \\
        h\tau_N         & h\tau_N & \dots       & h\tau_N   & \tau_N \\
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]
}

nodes.statement_short: Write out $\sum\lambda_iA_{i-1,i}$ and $\sum\tau_iD_i$ explicitly.

nodes.name: Conclude dual form
nodes.statement:
Finally,  using the relations (\ref{eqtau}) to eliminate $\tau_i$, and recalling that
$\mathrm{val}\!\eqref{P:agpr}$ was defined as $-LR^2 \mathrm{val}\!\eqref{P:gpr}$, the desired form of the stated dual problem
follows.

nodes.statement_short: Eliminate $\tau$ to obtain (DG').

nodes.name: Feasibility and relaxation
nodes.statement:
First note that both (G) and \eqref{P:gpr} are clearly feasible 
and $\mathrm{val} (G) \leq\mathrm{val}\eqref{P:gpr}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Weak duality
nodes.statement:
Invoking Lemma \ref{lem:dual}, by weak duality for the pair of primal-dual problems
\eqref{P:gpr} and \eqref{P:dualgpr}, we thus obtain that $\mathrm{val}\eqref{P:gpr}\leq \mathrm{val}\eqref{P:dualgpr}$

and hence:
\begin{equation} f(x_N)-f^* \leq \mathrm{val} (G) \leq \mathrm{val} \eqref{P:gpr} \leq \mathrm{val} \eqref{P:dualgpr}.
\end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.2 and weak duality, $f(x_N)-f^*\le\mathrm{val}(DG')$.

nodes.name: Dual candidate point
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\lambda_i=i/(2N+1-i)$ and $t=1/(2Nh+1)$.

nodes.name: Bound if feasible

Assuming that this point is \eqref{P:dualgpr}-feasible, it follows from (\ref{weak}) that
$$
f(x_N)-f^* \leq \mathrm{val}\eqref{P:dualgpr} \leq \frac{L R^2}{4 N h+2},
$$
which proves the desired result.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Reduce to feasibility
nodes.statement:
Thus, it remains to show that the above given choice
$(\lambda, t)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:dualgpr}. First, it is easy to see that all the linear constraints
of \eqref{P:dualgpr} on the variables $\lambda_i, i=1,\ldots ,N$ described through the set $\Lambda$
hold true.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: S is PSD
nodes.statement:
Now we prove that the matrix $S\equiv S(\lambda,t)$ is positive semidefinite. From
Lemma~\ref{L:positivedefinitea0a1}, with $h \in [0,1]$, we get that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1$ is
positive definite, as a convex combination of positive definite matrices. Next, we argue that
the determinant of $S$ is zero. Indeed, take $u:=(1,\dots,1,-(2Nh+1))^T$, then from the
definition of $S$ and the choice of $\lambda_i$ and $t$ it follows by elementary algebra that
$Su=0$. To complete the argument, we note that the determinant of $S$ can also be found via
the identity (see, e.g., \cite[Section~A.5.5]{boyd2004}):
\[
    \det(S) = (t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q) \det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1).
\]
Since we have just shown that  $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1 \succ 0$, then $\det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)>0$ and
we get from the above identity that the value of $t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q$, which is the
Schur complement of the matrix $S$, is equal to 0. By a well known lemma on the Schur
complement \cite[Lemma~4.2.1]{ben2001lectures}, we conclude that $S$ is positive semidefinite.

nodes.statement_short: Show $S(\lambda,t)\succeq0$.

nodes.statement:
From
Lemma~\ref{L:positivedefinitea0a1}, with $h \in [0,1]$, we get that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1$ is
positive definite, as a convex combination of positive definite matrices.

\]
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Recall the Schur-complement determinant formula.

nodes.name: Schur complement zero
nodes.statement:
Since we have just shown that  $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1 \succ 0$, then $\det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)>0$ and

By a well known lemma on the Schur

nodes.name: Plan and normalization
nodes.statement:
We will describe two functions that attain the two parts of the $\max$ expression in the above
claimed statement. For the sake of simplicity we will

assume that 
$L=1$ and $R=\|x_\ast-x_0\|=1$.
Generalizing this proof to general values of $L$ and $R$
can be done by an appropriate scaling.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Two functions, one per term of the max; WLOG $L=R=1$.

nodes.name: First term via Moreau envelope
nodes.statement:
To show the first part of the $\max$ expression, consider the function

\[
    \varphi_1(x) =
    \begin{cases}
        \frac{1}{2Nh+1} \|x\| -\frac{1}{2(2Nh+1)^2}       &   \| x \| \geq \frac{1}{2Nh+1} \\
        \frac{1}{2} \|x\|^2         &   \| x\| < \frac{1}{2Nh+1}
    \end{cases}.
\]
Note that this function is nothing else but the Moreau proximal envelope of the function
$\frac{1}{2Nh+1}\|x\|$, \cite{M65}. It is well known that this function is convex, continuously
differentiable with Lipschitz constant $L=1$, and that its minimal value $\varphi(x_*)=0$, see
e.g., \cite{M65, rock-wets-book98}. Applying the gradient method on $\varphi_1(x)$ with
$x_0=\nu$ where, as before, $\nu$ is a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we obtain that for $i=0,\dots,N$:
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \varphi_1^\prime(x_i) &=& \frac{1}{2N h+1}\nu;\;  x_i = \left(1-\frac{i h}{2N h+1}\right)\nu,\\
 \mbox{and}\; \varphi_1(x_i) &=&  \frac{1}{2N h+1}\left(1-\frac{h i}{2N h+1} \right)-\frac{1}{2(2N h+1)^2}\\
 &=& \frac{1}{4Nh+2} \left(\frac{4Nh+1-2hi}{2Nh+1}\right).
 \end{eqnarray*}
Therefore,
\[
    \varphi_1(x_N)-\varphi_1(x_\ast)  = \varphi_1(x_N) = \frac{1}{4 N h+2}.
\]
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: First term attained by a Huber-type function.

nodes.name: Define phi_1
nodes.statement:
To show the first part of the $\max$ expression, consider the function

\[
    \varphi_1(x) =
    \begin{cases}
        \frac{1}{2Nh+1} \|x\| -\frac{1}{2(2Nh+1)^2}       &   \| x \| \geq \frac{1}{2Nh+1} \\
        \frac{1}{2} \|x\|^2         &   \| x\| < \frac{1}{2Nh+1}
    \end{cases}.
\]
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Define the Huber-like $\varphi_1$.

nodes.name: Properties of phi_1
nodes.statement:
Note that this function is nothing else but the Moreau proximal envelope of the function
$\frac{1}{2Nh+1}\|x\|$, \cite{M65}. It is well known that this function is convex, continuously
differentiable with Lipschitz constant $L=1$, and that its minimal value $\varphi(x_*)=0$, see
e.g., \cite{M65, rock-wets-book98}.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_1$ is a Moreau envelope, hence convex and 1-smooth with minimum 0.

nodes.name: GM iterates on phi_1
nodes.statement:
Applying the gradient method on $\varphi_1(x)$ with
$x_0=\nu$ where, as before, $\nu$ is a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we obtain that for $i=0,\dots,N$:
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \varphi_1^\prime(x_i) &=& \frac{1}{2N h+1}\nu;\;  x_i = \left(1-\frac{i h}{2N h+1}\right)\nu,\\
 \mbox{and}\; \varphi_1(x_i) &=&  \frac{1}{2N h+1}\left(1-\frac{h i}{2N h+1} \right)-\frac{1}{2(2N h+1)^2}\\
 &=& \frac{1}{4Nh+2} \left(\frac{4Nh+1-2hi}{2Nh+1}\right).
 \end{eqnarray*}
Therefore,
\[
    \varphi_1(x_N)-\varphi_1(x_\ast)  = \varphi_1(x_N) = \frac{1}{4 N h+2}.
\]
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Compute the GM iterates and final gap $1/(4Nh+2)$.

nodes.name: Second term via quadratic
nodes.statement:
To show the second part of the $\max$ expression, we apply the gradient method on
\[
    \varphi_2(x) = \frac{1}{2} \|x\|^2
\]
with $x_0=\nu$. We then get that for $i=0,\dots,N$:
$$
    \varphi_2^\prime(x_i)= x_i;\;  x_i =(1-h)^i \nu;\; \varphi_2(x_i) = \frac{1}{2}(1-h)^{2i},
$$
and hence
\[
    \varphi_2(x_N)-\varphi_2(x_\ast) = \varphi_2(x_N) = \frac{1}{2} (1-h)^{2N}
\]
and the desired claim is proven.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: On $\frac12\|x\|^2$ GM gives gap $\frac12(1-h)^{2N}$.

nodes.name: Induction plan
nodes.statement:
We will show by induction that the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace is
identical to the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM}\xspace, and that the value of
$x_N$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace is equal to the value of $x_N$ generated by
Algorithm~\text{FGM}\xspace.
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: Plan: induction on the $y$ sequence, then $x_N$.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement:
First note that the sequence $t_i$ is defined by the two algorithms in the same way. Now let
$\{x_i$, $y_i\}$ be the sequences generated by \text{FGM}\xspace and denote by $\{y_i^\prime\}$,
$x_N^\prime$ the sequence generated by \text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace. Obviously, $y^\prime_1 = y_1$ and since
$t_1=1$ we get using the relations \ref{E:nesterovsteps}:
\begin{align*}
    y_2^\prime &= y_1^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(2)}_1 f^\prime(y_1^\prime) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} \left(1+\frac{t_{1}-1}{t_2} \right) f^\prime(y_1) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_1)= x_1 = y_2.
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: Same $t_i$; verify $y'_2=y_2$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
Assuming $y_i^\prime = y_i$ for $i = 1,\dots,n$, we then have
\begin{align*}
    y_{n+1}^\prime &= y_n^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_n f^\prime(y_n^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_{n-1} f^\prime(y_{n-1}^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} h^{(n+1)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\
        &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} (1+\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}) f^\prime(y_n) - \frac{1}{L} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}(h^{(n)}_{n-1}-1) f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\
        &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L}  f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime)\right) \\
        &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L}  f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) +y_n^\prime-y_{n-1}^\prime\right) \\
        &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} (x_n-x_{n-1}) \\
        &= y_{n+1}.
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: Expand the FO step sizes to show $y'_{n+1}=y_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Final iterate
nodes.statement:
Finally,
\[
    x_N^\prime = y_N^\prime -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N^\prime) = y_N -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N) = x_N.
\]
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: Then $x'_N=x_N$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement:
As (LIN) is a relaxation of \eqref{P:pblin}, it is enough to show that \eqref{P:pblin} can achieve the same
objective value.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show (BIL) attains the (LIN) value.

nodes.name: Case all lambda nonzero
nodes.statement:
Let $(r^\ast,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ be an optimal solution
for (LIN). If $\lambda_i^\ast \neq 0$ for all $1\leq i \leq N$, then~\eqref{E:solvebil}
satisfies all the equations in \eqref{E:definex} and therefore
$(h,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:pblin}.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: If all $\lambda_i^*\ne0$, (E:solvebil) solves (E:definex) and gives a feasible point.

nodes.name: Case some lambda zero
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\lambda^\ast_m=0$ for some $1\leq m \leq N$ and that $m$ is the maximal index with
this property. Then by the equality and non-negativity constraints in (LIN), we get that
$\lambda^\ast_1=\lambda^\ast_2=\dots=\lambda^\ast_m=0$ and
$\tau^\ast_0=\tau^\ast_1=\dots=\tau^\ast_{m-1}=0$.
Let $S:=S(r,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast)$, then by the positive semidefinite constraint in (LIN), we have $S \succeq 0$.
From the linear equalities connecting $\lambda$ and $\tau$ it follows that
\[
    S_{i,i}=\begin{cases}
            \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_1^\ast+\tau_0^\ast) = \lambda_1^\ast, &\quad i=1 \\
            \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_i^\ast+\lambda_{i-1}^\ast+\tau_{i-1}^\ast) = \lambda_i^\ast, &\quad i=2,\dots,N
        \end{cases},
\]
and we get that $S_{1,1}=\dots=S_{m,m}=0$. By the properties of positive semidefinite matrices we now get that $r_{i,k}^\ast=0$ for $i=1,\dots,m$ and $k=0,\dots,i-1$,
hence the set of equations \eqref{E:definex} with the chosen values of $h_k^{(i)}$ is consistent.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: If some $\lambda_m^*=0$, the corresponding $r^*$ vanish, so the equations stay consistent.

nodes.name: Vanishing multipliers
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\lambda^\ast_m=0$ for some $1\leq m \leq N$ and that $m$ is the maximal index with
this property. Then by the equality and non-negativity constraints in (LIN), we get that
$\lambda^\ast_1=\lambda^\ast_2=\dots=\lambda^\ast_m=0$ and
$\tau^\ast_0=\tau^\ast_1=\dots=\tau^\ast_{m-1}=0$.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: Maximal $m$ with $\lambda_m^*=0$ forces earlier $\lambda^*,\tau^*$ to vanish.

nodes.name: S is PSD
nodes.statement: Let $S:=S(r,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast)$, then by the positive semidefinite constraint in (LIN), we have $S \succeq 0$.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: Let $S=S(r,\lambda^*,\tau^*)\succeq0$.

nodes.name: Zero diagonal
nodes.statement:
From the linear equalities connecting $\lambda$ and $\tau$ it follows that
\[
    S_{i,i}=\begin{cases}
            \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_1^\ast+\tau_0^\ast) = \lambda_1^\ast, &\quad i=1 \\
            \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_i^\ast+\lambda_{i-1}^\ast+\tau_{i-1}^\ast) = \lambda_i^\ast, &\quad i=2,\dots,N
        \end{cases},
\]
and we get that $S_{1,1}=\dots=S_{m,m}=0$.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal entries $S_{ii}=\lambda_i^*$, hence zero for $i\le m$.

nodes.name: Off-diagonal vanish
nodes.statement:
By the properties of positive semidefinite matrices we now get that $r_{i,k}^\ast=0$ for $i=1,\dots,m$ and $k=0,\dots,i-1$,
hence the set of equations \eqref{E:definex} with the chosen values of $h_k^{(i)}$ is consistent.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: PSD with zero diagonal forces $r^*_{i,k}=0$, so (E:definex) is consistent.

nodes.name: Statement of goal
nodes.statement:
We now establish the positive definiteness of the matrices $S_0$ and $S_1$
given in \eqref{b0matrix} and \eqref{b1matrix}, respectively.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3.3
nodes.statement_short: Prove $S_0\succ0$ and $S_1\succ0$.

nodes.name: S_0 positive definite
nodes.statement:
\subsection{$S_0 \succ 0$}
We begin by showing that $S_0$ is positive definite. Recall that
\[
    S_0=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        2 \lambda_1     & -\lambda_1            \\
        -\lambda_1          & 2 \lambda_2   & -\lambda_2                \\
            &       -\lambda_2          & 2 \lambda_3   & -\lambda_3                \\
                                    &        & \ddots        &\ddots &   \ddots\\
                                            & &                 &       -\lambda_{N-1}  & 2 \lambda_N & -\lambda_N \\
                                            & &                 &        &  -\lambda_N  & 1\\
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
for
\begin{align*}
    \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N.
\end{align*}

Let us look at $x^T S_0 x$ for any $x=(x_0,\dots,x_N)^T$:
\begin{align*}
    x^T S_0 x
        &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} 2\lambda_{i+1} x_i^2 -2\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} x_i x_{i+1} + x_N^2\\
        &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} (x_{i+1}-x_i)^2 +\lambda_1 x_0^2+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} (\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i) x_i^2+(1-\lambda_N)x_N^2
\end{align*}
which is always positive for $x\neq 0$. We conclude that $S_0$ is positive definite.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3.3
nodes.statement_short: Write $x^TS_0x$ as a sum of nonnegative squares with positive weights.

nodes.name: S_1 positive definite
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3.3
nodes.statement_short: Sylvester's criterion via closed-form leading principal minors.

nodes.name: Setup for S_1
nodes.statement:
We will show that $S_1$ is positive definite using Sylvester's criterion\footnote{Despite
the interesting structure of the matrix $S_1$, this proof is quite involved. A simpler proof
would be most welcome!}.

Recall that
\[
    S_1=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        2 \lambda_1         & \lambda_2-\lambda_1           &\dots          &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1}    &1-\lambda_N  \\
        \lambda_2-\lambda_1         & 2 \lambda_2                   &          &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1}    &1-\lambda_N \\

        \vdots & & \ddots & &\vdots \\
        \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1}     & \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1}   &          & 2\lambda_N    & 1-\lambda_N  \\
        1-\lambda_N         & 1-\lambda_N       & \dots         & 1-\lambda_N   & 1 \\
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
for
\begin{align*}
    \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N.
\end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3.3
nodes.statement_short: Recall $S_1$ and plan to use Sylvester's criterion.

nodes.name: Determinant recursion
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{A recursive expression for the determinants}
We begin by deriving a recursion rule for the determinant of matrices of the following form:
\[
    M_k=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        d_0 &   a_1 &   a_2 &       \dots   &   a_{k-1} &   a_k \\
        a_1 &   d_1 &   a_2 &               &   a_{k-1} &   a_k \\
        a_2 &   a_2 &   d_2 &                   &   a_{k-1} &   a_k \\
        \vdots  &   &   &   \ddots  & & \vdots\\
        a_{k-1} &   a_{k-1} & a_{k-1}   &                   &   d_{k-1} &   a_k \\
        a_k &   a_k &   a_k &   \dots       &   a_k     &   d_k
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]

To find the determinant of $M_k$,
subtract the one before last row multiplied by $\frac{a_{k}}{a_{k-1}}$ from the last row: the last row becomes
\[
    (0,\dots,0,a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1},d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}).
\]
Expanding the determinant along the last row we get
\[
    \det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1}-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det (M_k)_{k,k-1}
\]
where $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ denotes the $k,k-1$ minor:
\[
    (M_k)_{k,k-1}=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        d_0 &   a_1 &   a_2 &       \dots   &   a_{k-2} &   a_k \\
        a_1 &   d_1 &   a_2 &               &   a_{k-2} &   a_k \\
        a_2 &   a_2 &   d_2 &                   &   a_{k-2} &   a_k \\
        \vdots  &   &   &   \ddots  \\
        a_{k-2} &   a_{k-2} & a_{k-2}   &                   &   d_{k-2} &   a_k \\
        a_{k-1} &   a_{k-1} & a_{k-1}   &                   &   a_{k-1} &   a_k
    \end{pmatrix}
    .
\]
If we multiply the last column of $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ by $\frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}$
we get a matrix that is different from $M_{k-1}$ by only the corner element.
Thus by basic determinant properties we get that
\[
    \frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}\det (M_k)_{k,k-1} = \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k-1}-d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}.
\]
Combining these two results, we have found the following recursion rule for $\det M_k$, $k\geq 2$:
\begin{align*}
    &\det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1} \\&\qquad -(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1})\left(\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}} \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k}-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}\right) \\
            &= \left((d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k})-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}\right) \det M_{k-1} -\left(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}\right)^2\det M_{k-2}
\end{align*}
or
\begin{equation} \det M_k= \left(d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \right) \det M_{k-1}-a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \det M_{k-2} .
\end{equation}
Obviously, the recursion base cases are given by
\begin{align*}
    & \det M_0 = d_0, \\
    & \det M_1 = d_0 d_1-a_1^2.
\end{align*}
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3.3
nodes.statement_short: Row operations give a three-term recursion (E:mrecursion) for $\det M_k$.

nodes.name: Closed form
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3.3
nodes.statement_short: Identify $M_k$ with leading minors of $S_1$ and state closed forms for $\det M_k$.

nodes.name: Verification
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3.3
nodes.statement_short: Check base cases and that the closed forms satisfy the recursion.

nodes.name: Conclude via Sylvester
nodes.statement:
To complete the proof, note that the closed form expressions for $\det M_k$ consist of sums
and products of positive values, hence $\det M_k$ is positive, and thus follows from
Sylvester's criterion that $S_1$ is positive definite.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma~3.3
nodes.statement_short: All minors positive, so $S_1\succ0$.
